newsitem.title: UK: Fertilizer enhancer developed from oyster shells.
newsitem.headline: Fertilizer enhancer developed from oyster shells.

text.p: A company in America has developed what is thought to be the world's first fertilizer-enhancer, using a polymer derived from oyster shells, New Scientist magazine reported on Thursday.
The polymer helps plant roots to absorb nutrients from the surrounding soil and can boost crop yields by around five percent without farmers having to apply extra fertilizer.

"I think this compound is the first legitimate fertilizer enhancer. It allows plants to grow at levels of nutrients, five to tenfold lower than normal," Fred Below, professor of plant physiology at the University of Illinois told New Scientist.
The polymer, polyaspartic acid, also helps keep down contamination of rivers and waterways by soaking up phosphorus and nitrogen from fertilizer that would otherwise seep out of the soil.
But Below said his test results were erratic and varied with soil temperature, salinity, soil condition and the amount of sunlight the crops received.
"I think it works best in low to moderately fertile soil with low phosphorus," he said.

The unusual properties of the polyaspartic acid were discovered by Professor Hap Wheeler of Clemson University in South Carolina, who discovered that oysters control the growth and shape of their shells by regulating the amount of polymer that is deposited.
"We found that the polymer could inhibit mineral growth as well as promoting it," Wheeler said.
Researchers from the Donlar company of Illinois followed up Wheeler's findings to discover that the polymer also helps plants to extract nutrients.
Donlar, which was originally set up to develop polyaspartic acid as a coating to block corrosion and the formation of scale on marine structures, now produces a man-made version of the polymer.
